title: Build a Reasoning Model: a coding course for measuring how reasoning methods work
entity: Build a Reasoning Model (From Scratch) video course
summary: Eight coding videos connect Qwen3 generation, answer verification, inference scaling, reinforcement learning and distillation, with public code and realistic compute caveats.

sections.title: An inspectable route from a base model to reasoning experiments
sections.html:
Sebastian Raschka’s October 24, 2026 announcement gathers eight coding videos covering more than eleven hours. The series accompanies Build a Reasoning Model (From Scratch), moving through generation, evaluation, inference-time scaling, reinforcement learning, and distillation in Python and PyTorch. The new event is the video course; its companion book and repository already existed.

Learners start with pretrained Qwen3-0.6B and inspect how different interventions change its outputs. Generating more candidates, selecting answers differently, and updating weights have different costs and failure patterns. A verifier introduced early later supplies training rewards, connecting evaluation to learning.

The course guide defines the sequence, while the official repository provides code and exercises. Its stated purpose is a small educational reasoning model. The practical value is understanding and measuring the components, without expecting the resulting checkpoint to reproduce a frontier training system.

sections.title: Eight videos with a measurement thread
sections.html:
Video one covers setup, dependencies, hardware, and environment problems. Video two loads Qwen3-0.6B and implements streaming generation, key-value caching, and compilation. This provides a foundation for distinguishing faster execution from better answers.

Video three builds a math-answer verifier through extraction, normalization, and equivalence checks, then evaluates on MATH-500. Because that verifier later determines rewards, its mistakes matter: a parser can reject an equivalent answer, while permissive checking can reward an invalid one. Math verification does not automatically extend to subjective explanations or creative work.

Videos four and five keep weights fixed while exploring sampling, temperature, top-p filtering, self-consistency through voting, scoring, and self-refinement. The useful comparison is answer quality alongside the extra generations needed to obtain it.

Videos six and seven implement reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards using simplified Group Relative Policy Optimization, then add diagnostics, clipped policy ratios, and KL terms. Video eight covers teacher-response distillation, data preparation, supervised training, and evaluation; the announcement names DeepSeek R1 in its teacher-data example. These are documented curriculum topics, not independently reproduced results.

sections.title: Start small enough to explain every failure
sections.html:
For a first educational project, build a notebook recording each question, response, extracted answer, verifier result, elapsed time, and generation settings. Establish one baseline on a small sample and inspect failures before adding complexity. Then change one variable, such as the number of sampled candidates, and compare paired examples while recording inference effort.

In a class, pairs could investigate extraction errors, voting outcomes, or refinement that damaged an initially correct answer. Ask for an experiment card stating the hypothesis, baseline, intervention, evaluation set, compute budget, and largest unresolved failure. Include examples selected before seeing results as well as examples chosen to explain errors.

Later training exercises should preserve held-out evaluation data and stable evaluation procedures. Distillation additionally calls for inspecting teacher outputs and separating training, validation, and test data. These classroom proposals adapt the course’s components; the sources do not establish their learning effectiveness or present them as the author’s assignments.

Keep formatting, verification, and reasoning failures separate. An apparently correct result can conceal an unreliable process, while a useful response can be rejected by answer extraction. Comparing these cases helps students explain an aggregate score. When methods appear tied, response length, runtime, and failure type can still provide useful distinctions, provided the evaluation conditions stay consistent.

sections.title: Turning the code into useful educational interfaces
sections.html:
An app or website project could turn the early chapters into an experiment viewer. Show a problem beside candidate answers, extracted results, and the selection rule. Let learners compare one response with several under a fixed budget, retaining previous settings and results. The repository lists optional chat-interface material, but this experiment viewer is an editorial proposal, not a promised course feature. A deployed service would still need its own reliability and user-experience work.

For educational video, demonstrate why caching changes runtime, follow an answer from raw output to reward, and compare successful refinement with a case that worsens the answer. Display the model, dataset, hardware, and settings so viewers can interpret the demonstration.

Product teams can also use these components to explore sampling and selection when a dependable verifier exists. For tutoring, final-answer correctness remains an incomplete objective: explanation quality, learner understanding, and intervention timing need separate evaluation. The course supplies foundations for those investigations, not evidence of improved learning outcomes.

sections.title: Hardware, access, and the meaning of open code
sections.html:
Raschka recommends familiarity with Python and PyTorch. His preceding LLM-from-scratch course is recommended but optional. This sequence begins with pretrained weights, so learners can focus on reasoning methods rather than implementing complete pretraining.

The repository says chapters two through four work on CPUs and GPUs, recommending a GPU to reproduce chapters five and six. Its setup guide says NVIDIA GPUs can substantially improve runtime, especially in chapters five through seven. These are author recommendations; no exact memory minimum, runtime budget, or successful installation was independently verified here.

Lightning AI Studio and Google Colab appear as optional cloud environments. Current prices, quotas, and total execution costs were not established. Publicly accessible materials do not imply that every training experiment is free to run. Start by checking the selected notebook’s dependencies and local feasibility before choosing cloud compute.

The companion code is Apache-2.0 licensed. That supports studying and adapting it subject to the license conditions, but does not establish identical rights for the book, videos, model weights, datasets, or teacher-generated material. The book is an optional companion for deeper explanations and exercises; no purchase price is asserted.

sections.title: The lesson is experimental control, not a model ranking
sections.html:
The small-model math setting limits generalization. MATH-500 gains do not establish improvements in coding, factual reliability, or tutoring. Higher reward can reflect verifier behavior rather than broader reasoning ability; the curriculum’s discussion of reward hacking and training diagnostics makes this a useful question to investigate.

Compare quality with the work required to obtain it. Voting generates multiple answers, refinement adds model calls, reinforcement learning requires rollouts and updates, and distillation requires teacher data and training. No method is shown here to be universally cheaper or better.

Record code revision, environment, checkpoint, dataset version, and settings for reproducibility. This report executed no commands or notebooks, downloaded no models or training data, and did not watch the full lecture series. Its recommendation rests on the documented curriculum and inspectable code. The worthwhile outcome is a learner who can explain what changed, where it failed, and what it cost; controlled evidence of educational effectiveness remains absent.

useCases: Build a measurable reasoning-model lab for Python and PyTorch students.
Create experiment viewers that expose candidate selection and verifier decisions.
Make educational videos comparing reasoning methods with reproducible examples.
limitations: No notebooks, training runs or model downloads were executed.
Small-model math examples do not establish general-purpose or tutoring effectiveness.
GPU runtime and end-to-end cost depend on experiment settings and were not measured.
Apache-2.0 code does not establish identical terms for book, videos, models or datasets.

judgment: A concrete educational pathway for understanding and evaluating reasoning techniques; useful because its components can be inspected and varied, not because it promises a frontier model.
researchNote: Course announcement, official repository README, setup index and GPU guidance inspected in Chrome and archived. Curriculum descriptions are documented rather than independently tested; the full lecture series was not watched. Proposed classroom, interface and video projects are editorial adaptations.
